forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Stockport expects £61.065m grant on 30 November, covering 90% of eligible historic SEND deficits
news_drafts.lead:
Stockport Council expects to receive £61.065m from the government on 30 November 2026 through the High Needs Stability Grant. The sum is 90% of eligible historic deficits, according to the mid-year treasury management report before its Corporate, Resource Management & Governance Scrutiny Committee on 24 November.

The paper says the grant addresses deficits on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, as they stood at 31 March 2026. It says those deficits arose mainly from spending on special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) above the funding received.

The report lists £49.141m of the receipt for settlement and £11.924m for temporary borrowing. The council says it has already used borrowing to cover the cashflow impact, so the receipt is not surplus cash.
news_drafts.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy and Annual Investment Strategy Mid-Year Review Report 2026/27

news_drafts.headline: Stockport says risk of seeking exceptional government support is rising, but not planned for 2027/28
news_drafts.lead:
Stockport Council's chief finance officer (its section 151 officer, the person with a legal duty to warn if the council cannot balance its books) has told the Corporate, Resource Management & Governance Scrutiny Committee that the risk of the council needing exceptional financial support is increasing. That is government permission to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending, and it is a last resort. The council does not intend to seek it for 2027/28.

The papers say this follows a "disappointing" multi-year funding settlement, which they say "materially weakened" the council's financial position. They also describe the underlying funding for essential local services as insufficient. The Summer Review of the council's medium-term financial plan says its ability to absorb further pressures is "increasingly constrained". It adds that the pressures "cannot be managed indefinitely through local measures alone". The council says they cannot be met by local efficiency measures alone and need sustainable national funding and policy reform. The same papers put the likelihood of a Section 114 notice, a formal warning that the council cannot balance its budget, as low in the short term.

For context, the papers cite the Local Government Association, which represents councils. It reports that 36 councils were granted exceptional financial support to set balanced budgets in 2026/27. It also warns that councils in England face a £7bn funding gap within three years. It attributes this to rising demand and costs in homelessness, children's services, adult social care, home-to-school transport and new national requirements.
news_drafts.paper_title: Part B Cabinet Response: Responding to Our Medium Term Financial Plan

news_drafts.headline: Stockport papers cite £5.6bn government funding to cover 90% of council SEND deficits to 2025/26
news_drafts.lead:
A Labour Group amendment before Stockport's Council Meeting on 1 October 2026 calls on government to fund council deficits caused by demand-led services that councils are required by law to provide. It points to what government has already done on one of them: around £5.6bn "to cover 90% of council SEND deficits built up to 2025/26, and a commitment to fund SEND centrally from 2028".

SEND stands for special educational needs and disabilities. Support for it is paid from the high needs part of school funding, the money for children with those needs, and it is one of the council's major cost pressures. The £5.6bn is a national figure covering councils across England. The material does not give Stockport's own share of it, or the size of the council's SEND deficit.

Under the commitment cited in the amendment, government would pay for SEND centrally from 2028 onwards, rather than councils meeting the cost from their own budgets. The material does not record the outcome of the vote on the amendment.
news_drafts.paper_title: Calling on government to fund council deficits caused by statutory demand-led services (Labour Group amendment)

findings.committee: Corporate, Resource Management & Governance Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy and Annual Investment Strategy Mid-Year Review Report 2026/27
findings.headline: Council must address a £12.078m savings requirement in 2027/28 and a projected £29.137m budget gap to 2030/31
findings.detail: The paper says the treasury strategy for 2027/28 must support the updated Medium-Term Financial Plan, which has these figures. It says the council's capacity to absorb treasury volatility is constrained, and the strategy will avoid relying on favourable market moves.
findings.matters: A stated savings requirement and medium-term gap set the scale of the budget problem that treasury decisions, including debt repayment, are meant to ease.
findings.figures: £12.078m savings requirement in 2027/28; £29.137m projected budget gap to 2030/31
findings.quote: This will include the need to address a savings requirement of £12.078m in 2027/28 and a projected budget gap of £29.137m over the medium-term up until 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy and Annual Investment Strategy Mid-Year Review Report 2026/27
findings.headline: Investment return averaged 3.87% in the first half of 2026/27, against average SONIA of 3.73% and a 3.40% budget assumption
findings.detail: The paper says the return was higher because Bank Rate stayed at 3.75%, and that funds were held mainly in instant-access money market funds. It adds that the investment gain was more than offset by higher borrowing costs for a net borrower.
findings.matters: Investment income above budget is a mid-year income variance, and the paper's offset against higher borrowing costs is relevant to how peers net the two.
findings.figures: 3.87% average return; 3.73% average SONIA; 3.40% budget assumption; average balance £22.355m
findings.quote: The council achieved an average investment return of 3.87% during the first half of 2026/27, compared with average SONIA of 3.73%.

findings.committee: Corporate, Resource Management & Governance Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy and Annual Investment Strategy Mid-Year Review Report 2026/27
findings.headline: The borrowing-funded element of the 2026/27 capital financing plan rose by £5.654m, even as the overall programme fell
findings.detail: The paper says grants and other non-borrowing funding fell by more than planned expenditure, so the borrowing requirement went up. The 2026/27 borrowing requirement is now £61.104m against an original £55.450m.
findings.matters: A fall in grant or capital funding that raises the borrowing requirement is a direct effect on a council's external borrowing need.
findings.figures: £5.654m increase in borrowing-funded element; £61.104m latest borrowing requirement; £55.450m original
findings.quote: Compared with the original plan, the borrowing-funded element has increased by £5.654m.

findings.committee: Corporate, Resource Management & Governance Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy and Annual Investment Strategy Mid-Year Review Report 2026/27
findings.headline: Capital expenditure to 30 September 2026 was £65.638m, 46% of the latest 2026/27 programme
findings.detail: The paper says capital delivery is normally weighted to the second half of the year, and that some further rephasing into 2027/28 is likely. It says that would reduce the immediate cash requirement while leaving the underlying financing need to the following year.
findings.matters: Mid-year spend against a full-year programme is an early indicator of slippage that finance directors and lenders watch.
findings.quote: Actual and accrued capital expenditure to 30 September 2026 was £65.638m, representing 46% of the latest 2026/27 programme of £141.863m.
